e-4422.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Switching Two Rows
e-4422.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix and $\det (A) = -16.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$ (switching the first and the second rows). What is the value of $\det(B)?$
e-4422.worked_solution:
Since swapping any two rows changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite sign, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =-det(A) \\  & =-(-16) \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

e-4423.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Row by a Number
e-4423.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $6 \times 6$ matrix and $\det(A) = 32.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_3:= \dfrac{1}{8} R_3$. What is the value of $\det(B)?$
e-4423.worked_solution:
The row operation applied to $A$ consists of multiplying a row by the number $\dfrac{1}{8}.$

When we do this, the determinant is multiplied by the same number. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =\frac{1}{8}det(A) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot 32 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

e-6148.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Matrix by a Scalar
e-6148.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $4\times4$ matrix and $\det(A)=5.$ What is the value of $\det(2A)?$
e-6148.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A)={k}^{n}\cdot det(A).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=2$ and $n=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(2A) & ={2}^{4}\cdot det(A) \\  & =16\cdot 5 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

e-4424.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Applying Several Elementary Operations
e-4424.problem: Suppose $A$ is an $8 \times 8$ matrix and $\det(A) = 5.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operations $R_4 \leftrightarrow R_5,$ $R_6:= 4 R_6,$ and $R_8: = R_8 - \dfrac{1}{2} R_7.$ What is the value of $\det(B)?$
e-4424.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation $R_4 \leftrightarrow R_5$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation $R_6:= 4 R_6$ involves multiplying a row by $4,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $4$ as well.

- The operation $R_8:= R_8 - \dfrac{1}{2} R_7$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $4$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =4\cdot (-det(A)) \\  & =-4det(A) \\  & =-4\cdot 5 \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$

e-6143.knowledge_point: Identifying a Row Operation Given the Connection Between Two Determinants
e-6143.problem:
Given that $\det(X)=\det(Y),$ which elementary row operations transforms matrix $X$ to matrix $Y,$ where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082528/assets/fd6c1665506e5186c1ccac2cf669040943bbc31347b27fae1c77ffe9b01ed542.png)
e-6143.worked_solution:
Since $\det(X)=\det(Y)$, the row operation applied to $X$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
R_j := R_j + (k)R_i, \quad i \neq j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(X) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{3} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(Y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
R_2:= R_2 + 3R_3.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot C)={k}^{n}\cdot det(C).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}det(3C) & =(-3)^{4}\cdot det(C) \\  & =81\cdot 5 \\  & =405.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Matrix by a Scalar
content.problem: Suppose $Y$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $det(Y)=2.$ What is the value of $det(-4Y)?$
content.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot Y)={k}^{n}\cdot det(Y).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=-4$ and $n=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(-4Y) & =(-4)^{3}\cdot det(Y) \\  & =-64\cdot 2 \\  & =-128.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Suppose $X$ is a $6\times 6$ matrix and $det(X)=39.$ The matrix $Y$ is obtained from $X$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{4}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{4}$ and ${R}_{5}:={R}_{5}+(-3){R}_{1}.$ What is the value of $det(Y)?$
after.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{5}:={R}_{5}+(-3){R}_{1}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{4}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{4}$ involves multiplying a row by $\frac{1}{3},$ so the determinant is multiplied by $\frac{1}{3}$ as well.

Therefore, we only have to multiply the determinant by $\frac{1}{3}.$ Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Y) & =\frac{1}{3}det(X) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 39 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose U is a 4×4 matrix and det(U)=21. The matrix V is obtained from U by applying the elementary row operations R3:=R3+(−7)R4 and R3:=13R3. What is the value of det(V)?

a
−5
b
3
c
7
d

−9

EXPLANATION

First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

  • The operation R3:=R3+(−7)R4 involves adding a multiple of one row to another row, so it does not change the determinant.

  • The operation R3:=13R3 involves multiplying a row by 13, so the determinant is multiplied by 13 as well.

Therefore, we only have to multiply the determinant by 13. Consequently, we get

det(V)=13det(U)=13⋅21=7.

verification.explanation: Adding a multiple of another row leaves the determinant unchanged; scaling row 3 by 1/3 multiplies it by 1/3. Thus det(V) = 21/3 = 7, confirming the worked solution.

content.problem: Suppose $U$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $det(U)=21.$ The matrix $V$ is obtained from $U$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-7){R}_{4}$ and ${R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(V)?$
content.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-7){R}_{4}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{3}$ involves multiplying a row by $\frac{1}{3},$ so the determinant is multiplied by $\frac{1}{3}$ as well.

Therefore, we only have to multiply the determinant by $\frac{1}{3}.$ Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(V) & =\frac{1}{3}det(U) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 21 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 8 & -1 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}]?
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 8 & -1 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3}.
$$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}]?
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}| & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{3} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{3}.
$$
